decisions.title: Adopt PEP 709 as a whole
decisions.summary: PEP 709 was adopted as a whole, with the intention to inline comprehensions occurring inside functions where fast-locals are used, and to handle generator expressions as a follow-up.
decisions.rationale: The proposal was well-received by the community, with no significant objections raised. The author, Carljm, addressed concerns and updated the PEP accordingly.

decisions.title: Inlining of generator expressions
decisions.summary: The decision is still open on whether to inline generator expressions.
decisions.rationale: There is ongoing discussion about the feasibility and benefits of inlining generator expressions, given their potential for optimization and the associated costs.

evidence.quote: I have a question about generator expressions which are not mentioned in the PEP. I guess it’s probably more difficult but there could perhaps be greater potential for optimisation if a locally used generator expression did not need to have an actual generator function with associated per-yield frame-switching cost.
evidence.author: oscarbenjamin

evidence.quote: The intent is not to change them at all in this PEP. In general they are more difficult to inline, because the generator may escape, and if so it needs to be a real resumable generator function. But you’re right that in many cases where we know the generator does not escape (e.g. something like `tuple(x for x in lst)`) we can avoid generator overhead. If PEP 709 is merged, the most straightforward approach would be to convert such comprehensions at compile time to (inlined) list comprehensions, and then e.g. introduce a fast path for list-to-tuple conversion.
evidence.author: carljm

evidence.quote: I pushed an update to the PEP which addresses this. I realized that although the reference implementation doesn’t inline any generator expressions, the PEP should be clear that this is planned as a likely follow-up.

evidence.quote:
What about other name collisions between the loop variable and other variables accessible in the function? For example, calling builtin functions: 

```
def f(lst):
    x = SomeClass([dir for dir in lst])
    # Calling the builtin dir()
    return dir(x)
```

or referencing global variables: 

```
result = 1
def f(lst):
    results = [calculate(result) for result in lst]
    if results[0] != result:
        ...
```

The change from NameError to UnboundLocalError suggests the semantics would change in these cases, as well.
evidence.author: thomas

evidence.quote: Great observation, I was wondering if someone would ask this  The semantics don’t change for these cases, but only because the implementation in the compiler also does a push/pop of its internal scope data, such that e.g. the variable is still treated as a global (`LOAD_GLOBAL` is used) in the outer scope, and treated as a local only in the inner scope.
evidence.author: carljm

evidence.quote: A PEP is supposed to encapsulate discussion around the idea, so yes, since it came up in the discussion it should probably be mentioned in the PEP
evidence.author: thomas

evidence.quote: I’ll add these details to the PEP.

decisions.title: Behavior changes for name collisions
decisions.summary: The behavior for name collisions does not change, as the implementation already handles scope correctly.
decisions.rationale: The implementation in the compiler already pushes and pops scope information for the variable when entering/leaving the comprehension, ensuring that semantics are maintained.

evidence.quote: The semantics don’t change for these cases, but only because the implementation in the compiler also does a push/pop of its internal scope data, such that e.g. the variable is still treated as a global (`LOAD_GLOBAL` is used) in the outer scope, and treated as a local only in the inner scope.
evidence.author: carljm

evidence.quote: The support for globals that I mentioned above already kicks in the same for this case (because it’s exactly the same case as far as the compiler is concerned; the only difference is whether that name exists in module globals at runtime.)
evidence.author: carljm

alternatives.name: Changing the behavior to reflect the scope changes
alternatives.reason: Would introduce unnecessary complexity and change the behavior of existing code.

evidence.quote: I debated whether to include these details (and similar ones regarding edge cases with cells) in the PEP. On the one hand, including all these details could reassure an observant reader of the PEP, such as yourself, that the necessary cases have been considered (and tested in the implementation) and semantics won’t change. On the other hand, I thought the purpose of the PEP was to evaluate the behavior changes it does cause, which means that implementation details involved in avoiding behavior changes in other edge cases might be an unnecessary distraction.
evidence.author: carljm

decisions.title: Inlining of comprehensions and its effect on debugging
decisions.summary: Inlining of comprehensions will not affect the debugger's ability to track the value of outer variables during comprehension execution.
decisions.rationale: Inlining comprehensions will not change the behavior of the debugger in terms of tracking the value of outer variables. The outer value of `x` will be stored on the stack while the comprehension is executing, and the debugger will not be able to query this value during comprehension execution.

evidence.quote: Yes, that should be the behavior.
evidence.author: carljm

evidence.quote: No, I don’t think this is feasible. In your example, the outer value of `x` will be stored only on the (interpreter’s value) stack while the comprehension is executing, and it’s likely not reasonable to expect pdb to figure out where on the stack it is and go look for it (not to mention that inspecting arbitrary stack locations isn’t part of the frame API exposed to Python, and also that it’s not clear what pdb command would even make sense for this operation.)
evidence.author: carljm

alternatives.name: Allowing the debugger to query the value of outer variables during comprehension execution
alternatives.reason: Not feasible due to the way the interpreter manages stack frames and the limitations of the debugger API.

decisions.title: Will async comprehensions be inlined?
decisions.summary: Async comprehensions will be inlined as part of the implementation.
decisions.rationale: The implementation automatically inlines async comprehensions without any additional handling, as they are orthogonal to inlining.

evidence.quote: It does. Async comprehensions are orthogonal to inlining, so it just falls out of the implementation without any additional handling.

decisions.title: Is the proposal a concern for Cython?
decisions.summary: The Steering Council has not explicitly decided if the PEP is a concern for Cython, but Cython developers are relaxed about it.
decisions.rationale: The Cython developers are not concerned about the changes described in the PEP, as they are mostly focused on Python 3.6 compatibility and the changes do not significantly impact Cython's functionality.
